title: Irrationality of √2
informal: √2 is irrational.
scope: `Irrational(√2)`, where `Irrational(x)` says that no rational `q ∈ ℚ` is sent to `x` by the embedding `rationalCut` of ℚ into ℝ: the textbook `√2 ∉ ℚ`, with ℚ read as its copy inside ℝ. The set form `√2 ∉ rationalReals` (the image of the embedding), the pointwise form `√2 ≠ rationalCut(q)`, and the quotient form `√2 ≠ p/q` for naturals `p` and `q ≠ 0` are stated as well. The proof shows the embedding is additive, carries multiplication by a natural, and sends a rational (a − b)/m to a real with `rationalCut(q)·m = a − b`; squaring reduces to the natural-number statement that no `p` and positive `q` satisfy `p² = 2q²`, proved by descent from the least such `p`.

title: Fundamental theorem of algebra
informal: Every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root.
scope: Root existence for every nonconstant polynomial over the concrete Dedekind-real complex field: in the monic form `complexes.fundamental_theorem_of_algebra`, in the general form with an explicit nonzero leading coefficient (`hornerAt` with lower coefficients `cs ≠ []`), and in the single-coefficient-list form where some coefficient of index at least one is nonzero. The general forms divide by the leading coefficient and reduce to the monic case. The proof inherits Global Choice through minimum attainment. Counting roots with multiplicity is a separate theorem, not proved here.

title: Denumerability of the rationals
informal: The rational numbers are countable.
scope: `Countable(ℚ)` means an injection from ℚ into ℕ exists. The proof injects ℕ × ℕ into ℕ by (a, b) ↦ 2^a(2b + 1), shows countability passes to subsets, products, and images under surjections (choosing the least code, without Choice), and applies this to the quotient construction of ℚ from pairs of naturals and a positive denominator.

title: Pythagorean theorem
informal: In a right triangle, c² = a² + b².
scope: Squared Euclidean distances over Dedekind reals; orthogonality expresses the right angle. Includes degenerate configurations. No square-root distance is needed.

title: Euler's generalization of Fermat's little theorem
informal: If gcd(a, n) = 1 then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n); for a prime p and p ∤ a, a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p).
scope: For naturals `a` and `n > 1` with `gcd(a, n) = 1`, `a^φ(n) % n = 1`, where `φ(n)` is the length of the list of residues below `n` coprime to `n`. The proof scales that list by `a`: the scaled entries have the same multiplicities as the original list (an inverse of `a` exists by a counting argument on residues), so their products agree, and the product of units is coprime to `n`, so it cancels. Fermat's little theorem `a^(p−1) % p = 1` for a prime `p ∤ a` follows from `φ(p) = p − 1`. The totient is defined by this count rather than by a product formula, and its multiplicativity is not proved.

title: Infinitude of primes
informal: For every natural bound there is a larger prime; the set of primes is infinite.
scope: Both order-unboundedness and the set-theoretic non-finiteness conclusion are proved.

title: Fundamental theorem of integral calculus
informal: For continuous f, differentiating x ↦ ∫ₐˣ f recovers f. A continuous derivative integrates to the endpoint difference.
scope: Riemann integration on real closed intervals. FTC-I is an interior derivative statement; the second displayed theorem assumes a continuous integrand and the stated local derivative hypotheses. No Lebesgue-integral generality is claimed.

title: Non-denumerability of the continuum
informal: The real numbers cannot be enumerated by the natural numbers.
scope: The carrier is the constructed Dedekind reals. The proof embeds the powerset of the naturals into the reals and uses Cantor diagonalization.

title: Formula for Pythagorean triples
informal: The primitive Pythagorean triples are exactly (m² − n², 2mn, m² + n²) with m > n > 0 coprime and of opposite parity, up to the order of the legs; every Pythagorean triple is a multiple of a primitive one.
scope: A Pythagorean triple is a triple of positive naturals with `a ^ 2 + b ^ 2 = c ^ 2`, primitive when `gcd(a, b) = 1`; "opposite parity" is `Odd(m + n)`. Both directions are proved over the naturals: `pythagorean.of_parameters` and `pythagorean.primitive_of_parameters` give the triples of the parametrization, `pythagorean.one_even` shows a primitive triple has exactly one even leg, and `pythagorean.primitive_form` recovers `m` and `n` for every primitive triple with `b` even, so every primitive triple up to swapping the legs. `pythagorean.form` writes any triple as `gcd(a, b)` times a primitive one. The arithmetic heart, that coprime factors of a square are squares, is `IsSquare.of_coprime_mul`, proved by the cofactor argument on `gcd(a, c)` without prime factorization. Everything is in ZF.

title: Schröder–Bernstein Theorem
informal: If there are injections from A into B and from B into A, then there is a bijection between A and B.
scope: Sets A and B with injective functions as graphs in both directions, written A ≼ B and B ≼ A. The bijection is built from the back-and-forth chain: f on the points of A reached from the complement of the image of g by iterating g ∘ f, and the inverse of g elsewhere.

title: The ballot problem
informal: If A receives a votes and B receives b < a votes, the orderings of the ballots in which A is strictly ahead throughout the count are (a − b)/(a + b) of all orderings.
scope: A ballot is 0 (a vote for A) or 1 (a vote for B), an ordering is a list over 2 read in the order of the count, `ballots(n)` is the set of such lists of length `n`, and `ballotSequences(a, b)` the lists of length `a + b` with `a` zeros along which every nonempty prefix holds more zeros than ones (`AlwaysAhead`). `ballot.count` gives `(a + b) * cardinality(ballotSequences(a, b)) = (a - b) * ((a + b) choose a)` for `b < a`, from the additive form `ballotSequences.count_succ`, `cardinality(ballotSequences(a + 1, b)) + ((a + b) choose (a + 1)) = (a + b) choose a` for `b ≤ a`, and the absorption identities of the binomial coefficients. The proof is the recursion by the first ballot: the orderings with `a` zeros and `b` ones along which A stays ahead by more than `k` split, by their first ballot, into the cons images of the families at `(k + 1, a − 1, b)` and `(k − 1, a, b − 1)`, and `leadSequences.closed_form` verifies `cardinality + (n choose (a + k + 1)) = n choose a` by induction on `n = a + b` with Pascal's rule; the ballot sequences are the case of a first ballot 0 followed by a lead above one. `orderings.count` gives `cardinality(orderings(a, b)) = (a + b) choose a` for all orderings, and `ballot.probability` the probability form `prob(uniformWeight(orderings(a, b)), ballotSequences(a, b)) = realNat(a - b) / realNat(a + b)` on the uniform space of all orderings. The counting module is in ZF.

title: Ramsey's theorem
informal: For every n, every infinite set S, and every colouring of the n-element subsets of S with finitely many colours, some infinite subset of S has all its n-element subsets the same colour; and among any six people, three are mutual acquaintances or three are mutual strangers.
scope: The infinite Ramsey theorem in full: for every natural `n`, every infinite set `S`, and every function `C` from the n-element subsets of `S` into a finite set of colours, there is an infinite `H ⊆ S` and a colour `c` with `C(U) = c` for every n-element subset `U` of `H` (`ramsey.infinite_colours`); `ramsey.infinite` is the two-colour form and `ramsey.infinite_numeral` the form for a numeral of colours. The proof is the classical induction on `n`: a chain of nested infinite sets, each homogeneous for the colouring induced by a chosen point, is built by recursion on ℕ with global choice, the infinite pigeonhole principle picks a colour that recurs infinitely often, and the least index of an (n + 1)-subset of the chosen points reduces it to the previous stage. The finite case R(3, 3) ≤ 6 is proved separately for simple graphs.

title: Divergence of the harmonic series
informal: The series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ⋯ diverges.
scope: The harmonic terms 1/(k+1) form a real sequence whose partial sums pass every real number and therefore have no limit. The proof is the classical doubling bound `2·S(2m) ≥ 2·S(m) + 1`, iterated to `2·S(mₖ) ≥ 2 + k`, combined with the Archimedean property of the Dedekind reals, which is proved here from the cut structure (`Real.below_natural`). Divergence is stated both as unboundedness of the partial sums and as nonconvergence of the sequence of prefix sums.

title: Taylor's theorem
informal: If f is n + 1 times differentiable on [a, b], then f(b) = ∑_{k ≤ n} f⁽ᵏ⁾(a)(b − a)ᵏ/k! + f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)(b − a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1)! for some ξ strictly between a and b.
scope: The Lagrange remainder form on a closed interval `[A, B]` with `A < B`, for `(f : ℝ → ℝ)`. The derivative is the function `f′` chosen from `HasDerivativeAt`, and `f⁽ᵏ⁾` is that derivative applied `k` times; the hypothesis is `∀ k ≤ n, ∀ X ∈ closedInterval(A, B), DifferentiableAt(f⁽ᵏ⁾, X)`, and the conclusion is written as on paper, `f(B) = ∑ k ≤ n, f⁽ᵏ⁾(A) * (B - A) ^ k / k! + f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(C) * (B - A) ^ (n + 1) / (n + 1)!`, the factorials read as reals and the sum being the library's `∑` over the term sequence `taylorTerms(f, A, B)`. Proved for every `n` by induction on the derivative of the Taylor approximant and the Cauchy mean value theorem; the `n = 0` instance is checked to read as the mean value theorem, `f(B) = f(A) + f′(C) * (B - A)`. The case `B < A` is not stated separately.

title: Brouwer fixed point theorem
informal: Every continuous map from a closed ball (here the cube [0, 1]ⁿ) to itself has a fixed point.
scope: Every continuous self-map of the unit cube `[0, 1]ⁿ` in the sup metric has a fixed point, for every dimension `n`, and the same for the product of simplices cut out of the cube by a block map (the strategy spaces of a finite game). The cube theorem is proved from Kuhn's cubical version of Sperner's lemma: the points of dyadic grids are labelled by comparing each with its image, Kuhn's lemma gives a completely labelled cell at every scale, and a coordinatewise convergent subsequence of the cells squeezes the limit into a fixed point. The transfer to products of simplices uses an explicit continuous retraction of the cube. General compact convex sets are not treated.

title: Solution of a cubic
informal: Cardano's formula: the roots of a cubic are given by radicals.
scope: Cardano's formula over the concrete Dedekind-real complex field. For the depressed cubic `x³ + px + q`, `cubic.cardano_root` shows `s + t` is a root whenever `s³ + t³ = −q` and `3st = −p`, and `cubic.cardano_pair` constructs such a pair for every `p` and `q`: `s` is a cube root of a root of the resolvent quadratic `W² + 27qW − 27p³` and `t = −p/(3s)`, or `p = 0` and `t` is a cube root of `−q`. `cubic.solution` depresses a general monic cubic by `x = y − a·v` with `3v = 1` and returns a root of that form. Division is written through explicit inverses, and the cube and square roots come from the quadratic-root theorem and the fundamental theorem of algebra.

title: Arithmetic mean/geometric mean
informal: For nonnegative reals a and b, √(ab) ≤ (a + b)/2.
scope: The two-variable inequality over the Dedekind reals, with the real square root from the least-upper-bound property. The general n-variable form is not proved.

title: Sum of the reciprocals of the triangular numbers
scope: Both the finite and the infinite forms over the Dedekind reals. The summands are the real sequence `triangularReciprocals` with term k equal to 2/((k + 1)(k + 2)) = 1/T_{k+1}; the partial sum of the first n terms is 2n/(n + 1), proved by telescoping, and `triangularReciprocals.sums_to` states that the series sums to 2, as the limit of the partial sums, from n/(n + 1) → 1.

title: The binomial theorem
informal: (a + b)ⁿ = Σₖ C(n, k) aᵏ bⁿ⁻ᵏ.
scope: For real `A`, `B` and every natural `n`, `(A + B)^n` equals the partial sum over `k < n + 1` of the terms `choose(n, k)·A^k·B^(n − k)`, with the binomial coefficient defined by Pascal's rule and the exponent `n − k` as truncated subtraction. The proof is by induction on `n`: Pascal's rule holds term by term, so splitting off the first term and reindexing the shifted sum turns the row `n + 1` into `A` times the row `n` plus `B` times the row `n`, where the extra top term vanishes because the coefficient above the diagonal is zero.

title: Solution of the general quartic equation
informal: Ferrari's method: the roots of a quartic are given by radicals through a resolvent cubic.
scope: Ferrari's method over the concrete complex field. `quartic.ferrari_identity` is the factorisation `4(y⁴ + py² + qy + r) = (2y² + p + 2m)² − (2αy − γ)²` under `α² = 2m`, `αγ = q`, `γ² = 4m² + 4pm + p² − 4r`; `quartic.depressed_solution` produces `m` from the resolvent cubic `8m³ + 8pm² + 2p²m − 8rm − q² = 0` through the cubic theorem, `α` and `γ` as above, and a root `y` of the quadratic `2y² − 2αy + (p + 2m + γ) = 0`, which is then a root of the quartic. `quartic.solution` depresses a general monic quartic by `x = y − a·e` with `4e = 1`. The statements give a root in formula form; the four roots with multiplicity are not enumerated.

title: The Cayley–Hamilton theorem
informal: Every square matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial.
scope: For a square matrix `M : R ^ n × n` over a bundled commutative ring `CommRing(R)`, the characteristic polynomial `charpoly(M)`, the element `det(X·1 − M)` of `polynomialRing(R, {0})`, evaluates at `M` to the zero matrix: `evalAt(M)(charpoly(M)) = matrixRing(R, n)[0]`, where `evalAt(M)` is the evaluation homomorphism `polynomialRing(R, {0}) →+* commutant(R, n, M)` sending `X` to `M` and the constants to the scalar matrices, and `commutant(R, n, M)` is the commutative subring of the matrix ring `matrixRing(R, n)` generated by `M` and the scalars, the bicommutant of `{M}`. The proof reads the adjugate identity of the characteristic matrix over that commutative ring entry by entry and contracts it against the columns of `M`. Everything is in ZF.

title: Wilson's theorem
informal: (p − 1)! ≡ −1 (mod p) for every prime p.
scope: Both directions. For every prime `p`, `((p − 1)! + 1) % p = 0`, stated in natural numbers, where `p - 1` is truncated subtraction; conversely a natural `n > 1` with `((n − 1)! + 1) % n = 0` is prime, and `wilson.characterization` states the equivalence for every `n > 1`. The residues `2, …, p − 2` are paired with their modular inverses, chosen by uniqueness: a residue is its own inverse only when it is `1` or `p − 1`, so the product of the middle residues is `1` modulo `p` by induction on the length of such paired lists, and the remaining factor `p − 1` contributes `−1`; the case `p = 2` is computed directly. For the converse, a proper divisor `d` of `n` divides `(n − 1)!` and hence `1`.

title: Number of subsets of a set
informal: A set with n elements has 2^n subsets.
scope: `HasCardinality(A, n)` gives `HasCardinality(𝒫(A), 2 ^ n)`, by induction on n: adjoining a fresh element x to A puts 𝒫(insert(x, A)) in bijection with the tagged disjoint union 𝒫(A) ⊎ 𝒫(A), through the map that records whether x is in a subset, so the count doubles.

title: Königsberg bridges problem
informal: No walk crosses each of the seven Königsberg bridges exactly once.
scope: Actual bridge identities and endpoint table, including parallel bridges; derived from a general finite multigraph parity obstruction. Indexed paths replace the source list presentation.

title: Product of segments of chords
informal: If two chords AB and CD of a circle meet at P, then PA·PB = PC·PD.
scope: Euclidean plane with coordinates. The point P lies on each chord's line as P = A + t(B − A), so the statement covers intersections inside and outside the circle alike. Proved through the power of a point: the dot product of the two segments at P equals the squared distance to the center less the squared radius, and the product of the segment lengths is the square root of the product of their squares.

title: Heron's formula
informal: The area of a triangle with side lengths a, b, c and semiperimeter s = (a + b + c)/2 is √(s(s − a)(s − b)(s − c)).
scope: Euclidean plane with coordinates. The area is half the absolute value of the cross product of two sides, the side lengths are square roots of squared distances, and the semiperimeter is half their sum. Proved through the squared form 16·area² = 2a²b² + 2b²c² + 2c²a² − a⁴ − b⁴ − c⁴, a polynomial identity in the coordinates.

title: Formula for the number of combinations
informal: An n-element set has C(n, k) subsets with k elements.
scope: A finite set with `n` elements has exactly `choose(n, k)` subsets with `k` elements, where `choose` is defined by Pascal's rule and `subsetsOfSize(A, k)` is the set of subsets of `A` of cardinality `k`. The proof is by induction on `n`: the `k + 1` element subsets of `insert(a, B)` are sent by the powerset split of entry 52 onto the disjoint sum of the `k + 1` element subsets of `B` (those avoiding `a`) and the `k` element subsets of `B` (those containing `a`, with `a` removed), and Pascal's rule adds the two counts. The symmetric identity `choose(n, k) = choose(n, n − k)` is not included.

title: Bézout's theorem
informal: For any integers a, b, there are integers u, v with ua + vb = gcd(a, b).
scope: Nonnegative GCD is returned as a natural and embedded into the quotient integers. Natural-input coefficients are also computed and proved correct. No equivalence with the source program is asserted.

title: Cantor's theorem
informal: No function from a set onto its powerset exists.
scope: For every set A and every f, f is not a surjection from A onto 𝒫(A). Proved by the diagonal set. The uncountability of 𝒫(ℕ) and of the reals (entry 22) build on it.

title: L'Hôpital's rule
informal: If f(a) = g(a) = 0, f and g are differentiable near a with g′ ≠ 0 away from a, and f′(x)/g′(x) → L as x → a, then f(x)/g(x) → L.
scope: The `0/0` form at a point, for `(f g : ℝ → ℝ)`, with limits as the library's punctured limit `TendsToAt` and quotients as `pointwiseDiv`: from `f(A) = 0`, `g(A) = 0`, `g′ ≠ 0` away from `A`, and `TendsToAt(pointwiseDiv(f′, g′), L, A)` follows `TendsToAt(pointwiseDiv(f, g), L, A)`. Differentiability is assumed on an open ball around `A`, including `A`; the Cauchy mean value theorem `CauchyMeanValue.theorem`, `f′(C) * (g(B) - g(A)) = g′(C) * (f(B) - f(A))`, proved from Rolle's theorem, gives for each `x` on either side of `A` a point strictly between where `f/g` equals `f′/g′`. The `∞/∞` form and limits at infinity are not covered.

title: Isosceles triangle theorem
informal: Equal legs give equal base angles.
scope: Euclidean plane. The cosine of an unoriented angle is the normalized dot product of its rays, proved to lie in [-1, 1]; an angle in [0, π] is determined by its cosine, so equal cosines are equal angles. The theorem states that the two base angles have equal cosines. The earlier root-free algebraic encoding (EqualAngle) is retained.

title: Sum of a geometric series
scope: Finite and infinite geometric sums over the Dedekind reals, as `realPartialSum` of the sequence of powers: the product form (1 − x)·Σ = 1 − xⁿ for every real x, the quotient form when 1 − x ≠ 0, and `geometricSeries.sums_to`: for |x| < 1 the series sums to 1/(1 − x), as the limit of the partial sums, from xⁿ → 0 by Bernoulli's inequality and the Archimedean property.

title: Sum of an arithmetic series
scope: Arbitrary real first term and common difference; the doubled formula avoids division, and a quotient-form corollary is also available.

title: Greatest common divisor algorithm
informal: The Euclidean algorithm returns the greatest common divisor.
scope: Structurally recursive remainder-based algorithm on arbitrary natural inputs, including zero. The integer wrapper uses absolute values. No running-time bound is claimed.

title: The perfect number theorem
informal: If 2^p − 1 is prime then 2^(p−1)(2^p − 1) is perfect (Euclid), and every even perfect number has this form (Euler).
scope: `sigma(n)` is the sum of the divisors of `n`, `natSum(divisors(n), identity(ℕ))` over the naturals, and `Perfect(n)` says `0 < n ∧ sigma(n) = 2 * n`. `perfect.of_mersenne` gives Euclid's direction for every `p` (primality of `2 ^ p - 1` already forces `p ≥ 2`), `perfect.even_form` gives Euler's converse as `∃ p ∈ ℕ, Prime(2 ^ p - 1) ∧ n = 2 ^ (p - 1) * (2 ^ p - 1)`, and `perfect.even_iff` combines them. Underneath: `sigma.multiplicative`, `sigma(m * n) = sigma(m) * sigma(n)` for `gcd(m, n) = 1`, proved through the bijection `(d, e) ↦ d · e` from `divisors(m) × divisors(n)` onto `divisors(m * n)` and the sum of products over a product set; `sigma.prime_iff`, `σ(p) = p + 1` characterises the primes above 1; and `sigma.two_pow`, `σ(2 ^ k) = 2 ^ (k + 1) - 1`, from `divisors(2 ^ (k + 1))` being 1 together with the doubles of `divisors(2 ^ k)`. Euler's direction writes `n = 2 ^ k · m` with `m` odd, reads `(2 ^ (k + 1) − 1) σ(m) = 2 ^ (k + 1) m`, and bounds the sum of the divisors strictly between 1 and `m`. Everything is in ZF.

title: Order of a subgroup
informal: Lagrange's theorem: the order of a subgroup of a finite group divides the order of the group.
scope: For a finite group `G` (one set with carrier, operation, unit, and inverse) and a subgroup `H`, `cardinality(H)` divides `order(G)`, the size of the carrier, and `order(G) = index(G, H) · cardinality(H)` with the index the number of left cosets `leftCosets(G, H)`. The proof is the textbook one: the cosets `g • H` partition the group (`leftCoset.eq_or_disjoint`, `leftCosets.cover`), each is in bijection with `H` by the translation `h ↦ g * h` (`leftCoset.cardinality`), and a disjoint union of equal blocks is counted by `cardinality.big_union_constant`. Independently of finiteness, `g ↦ (gH, rep(gH)⁻¹ · g)` is a bijection from the carrier onto `leftCosets(G, H) × H` (`Group.equipotent_cosets_product`); its representative is chosen with Global Choice. Normal subgroups and quotient groups are developed in their own modules.

title: Sylow's theorem
informal: A finite group of order p^k·m with p prime not dividing m has a subgroup of order p^k; every p-subgroup lies in a conjugate of it, any two Sylow p-subgroups are conjugate, and the number of Sylow p-subgroups divides m and is congruent to 1 modulo p.
scope: Over a bundled group `Group(G)` with `Finite(G)`, `Prime(p)`, `¬(p ∣ m)`, and `order(G) = p ^ k * m`: `sylow.exists_subgroup` gives `∃ P, Subgroup(P, G) ∧ cardinality(P) = p ^ k`; `sylow.subset_conjugate` gives `∃ g ∈ G, Q ⊆ conjugateSet(G, g, P)` for every `PSubgroup(Q, G, p)` and `SylowSubgroup(P, G, p)`; `sylow.conjugate` gives `∃ g ∈ G, Q = conjugateSet(G, g, P)` for two Sylow p-subgroups; `sylow.count_dvd` and `sylow.count_mod` give `cardinality(sylowSubgroups(G, p)) ∣ m` and `cardinality(sylowSubgroups(G, p)) % p = 1`. The proofs use group actions `act : G ↷ X` with orbits, stabilizers, and the orbit–stabilizer theorem `cardinality(orbit(x)) * cardinality(stabilizer(x)) = order(G)`: existence by the translation action on the subsets of size p^k, whose number `(p ^ k * m) choose (p ^ k)` is prime to p by Lucas' congruence; conjugacy by a p-subgroup acting on the cosets of a Sylow subgroup; the count by a Sylow subgroup acting on the Sylow subgroups by conjugation, with the class equation and the normalizer alongside.

title: Ascending or descending sequences
informal: Every sequence of mn + 1 distinct elements of a linear order has an increasing subsequence of length m + 1 or a decreasing one of length n + 1.
scope: The Erdős–Szekeres theorem. For a bundled linear order `LinearOrder(P)` and an injective `f : m * n + 1 → points(P)`, there is an index set `S ∈ subsetsOfSize(m * n + 1, m + 1)` with `IncreasingOn(P, f, S)` or one in `subsetsOfSize(m * n + 1, n + 1)` with `DecreasingOn(P, f, S)`, where `IncreasingOn` says `f(i) ≤ f(j)` for indices `i < j` of `S`. The proof labels each index with the length of the longest increasing run and of the longest decreasing run ending there, the latter as a run of the dual order; a later larger term lengthens the first label and a later smaller term the second, so the label pairs are distinct, and there are only m·n of them.

title: Principle of mathematical induction
informal: A set of natural numbers that contains 0 and is closed under successor contains every natural number.
scope: Stated for subsets of ℕ and proved by the least counterexample, using the least-element construction `leastNatural`. Structural induction on naturals is also a primitive kernel rule; this theorem derives the set-theoretic principle from Foundation.

title: Mean value theorem
informal: A real function continuous on [a, b] and differentiable inside has a point where its derivative equals its secant slope.
scope: Ordinary local derivative over the Dedekind reals. The formal conclusion uses multiplication by B-A instead of division.

title: Sum of kth powers
informal: Closed forms for 1ᵏ + 2ᵏ + ⋯ + nᵏ.
scope: Closed forms for the sums of the first n squares and cubes as real partial sums of `realNat` terms: `6·Σ i² = n(n+1)(2n+1)` and `4·Σ i³ = n²(n+1)²`, in multiplied-out form so no division is needed, together with Nicomachus's identity that the sum of the first n cubes is the square of the sum of the first n naturals (the latter is entry 68). Proofs are inductions closed by `linear_combination`. The general Faulhaber formula with Bernoulli numbers is not proved.

title: Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
informal: For finite-dimensional real vectors, ⟨u, v⟩² ≤ ⟨u, u⟩⟨v, v⟩.
scope: Arbitrary finite dimension, including zero, over real sequences restricted to their first n coordinates. Squared formulation with an exact equality criterion: the second vector has zero norm, or the first is a real scalar multiple of it on that prefix. No square-root norm is used.

title: Intermediate value theorem
informal: A continuous function on a closed interval takes every value between its values at the endpoints.
scope: Real functions `f : ℝ → ℝ` continuous on `closedInterval(A, B)` with `A ≤ B`. Both the strict form f(A) < V < f(B) and the form with ≤ are proved, together with the zero-crossing corollary; the point is the least upper bound of the set where f stays below V, so only Dedekind completeness is used. The symmetric case f(A) > V > f(B) follows by applying the theorem to −f and is not stated separately.

title: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic
informal: Every positive natural number is a product of primes, and the factorization is unique up to reordering.
scope: A factorization is a list of primes with product `∏ xs`; `n = 1` has the empty factorization. Uniqueness is stated as equality of multisets: two prime lists with the same product give every prime the same multiplicity. Euclid's lemma is derived through the integer Bézout identity. Everything is in ZF.

title: Divisibility by 3 rule
informal: A natural number is divisible by 3 exactly when the sum of its decimal digits is.
scope: Numbers are given by their decimal digits, least significant first, with `digitsValue` reading the list and `digitSum` adding it. The rule holds for any list of naturals, not only digits below ten, because every power of ten is one more than a multiple of three.

title: Derangements formula
informal: The number of permutations of n objects with no fixed point is d(n) = n! ∑_{k ≤ n} (−1)^k / k!, equivalently d(n) = ∑_{k ≤ n} (−1)^k (n choose k)(n − k)!, with d(n + 2) = (n + 1)(d(n + 1) + d(n)).
scope: `derangements(I)` is the set of permutations of `I` without a fixed point. `derangements.natural_count` gives `cardinality(derangements(n)) = derangement(n)` for the recurrence-defined sequence 1, 0, 1, 2, 9, 44, …, `derangements.recurrence` the textbook recurrence for the counts themselves, and `derangements.formula` the inclusion–exclusion sum in the integers, `integerOfNat(cardinality(derangements(n))) = derangementSum(n, n + 1)` with `derangementSum(n, k + 1) = derangementSum(n, k) + (−1)^k · (n choose k) · (n − k)!`, the integer form of n! ∑ (−1)^k/k!. The count is proved by the classical bijection: a derangement sends a chosen point a to some b, and either returns b to a, leaving a derangement of the other n − 2 points, or not, where composing with the transposition (a b) and forgetting a leaves a derangement of n − 1 points. The formula follows from the one-step recurrence d(n + 1) = (n + 1)d(n) + (−1)^(n + 1).

title: The factor and remainder theorems
informal: Dividing a polynomial p by X − a leaves the remainder p(a); a is a root exactly when X − a divides p.
scope: For a polynomial over any commutative ring, given by its Horner coefficient list, `remainder.theorem` is the synthetic-division identity `p(x) = p(a) + (x − a)·q(x)` with `q` the synthetic quotient, so the remainder on division by `X − a` is `p(a)`; `factor.theorem` specialises it at a root to `p(x) = (x − a)·q(x)`, and `factor.root` recovers the root from such a factorisation. Polynomials are concrete coefficient lists evaluated by Horner's rule, not elements of an abstract polynomial ring.

title: Triangle inequality
informal: ‖a − c‖ ≤ ‖a − b‖ + ‖b − c‖, and for real numbers |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|.
scope: Euclidean norm form in the plane: the distance between points is the square root of the squared distance, and the triangle inequality is proved from Cauchy–Schwarz. The real absolute-value and real-line metric forms are also checked. Higher-dimensional Euclidean space is not covered.

title: The birthday problem
informal: Among 23 people with independent, uniformly random birthdays in a year of 365 days, the probability that two share a birthday exceeds 1/2; for n people and d days it is 1 − d(d − 1)⋯(d − n + 1)/dⁿ.
scope: An assignment of birthdays to the people of `A` from the days of `B` is a function `A → B`, and `sharedBirthday(A, B)` is the set of assignments outside `injections(A, B)`; `sharedBirthday.membership` reads it as the assignments under which two distinct people get the same day. `birthday.counting` is the arithmetic core, `2 * fallingFactorial(365, 23) < 365 ^ 23`, certified by the kernel's closed-term evaluator through the equation `2 · 365·364⋯343 + 1 + c = 365²³` for the explicit 58-digit gap `c`. `birthday.injections` transfers it to any finite sets of 23 people and 365 days through `injections.count` and `functionSpace.count`: fewer than half of the assignments are injective. `sharedBirthday.probability` is the general formula on the uniform probability space of all assignments, `prob(uniformWeight(functionSpace(A, B)), sharedBirthday(A, B)) = 1 − realNat(fallingFactorial(|B|, |A|)) / realNat(|B| ^ |A|)` for finite `A` and finite nonempty `B`, from the complement rule of the uniform distribution; `birthday.problem` specializes it and bounds the quotient below 1/2 from the counting fact, giving `1/2 < prob(…)` as a real inequality. Every theorem's axiom audit lists only ZF axioms.

title: Law of cosines
informal: c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos γ.
scope: Euclidean plane, with side lengths that are square roots of squared distances and the cosine of the angle at the vertex defined as the normalized dot product of its rays, which is proved to lie in [-1, 1]. Requires the two rays to be nondegenerate. The root-free dot-product identity is retained.

title: Principle of inclusion/exclusion
informal: For finite sets, |A ∪ B| + |A ∩ B| = |A| + |B|.
scope: Two finite sets, with cardinality the natural number counting a finite set. The union splits as A with B ∖ A and B as A ∩ B with B ∖ A, two disjoint unions whose sizes add.

title: Cramer's rule
informal: A solution of a square linear system is given by ratios of determinants.
scope: Over a bundled commutative ring `CommRing(R)`, for a square matrix `M : R ^ n × n` and a solution `x` of the row system `x · M = b` (`rowProduct(R, n, x, M)(j) = b(j)` for every column `j`), `det(M) * x(i) = det(N)` where `N` is `M` with row `i` replaced by `b`; no division is assumed, so the statement holds over every commutative ring and gives `x(i) = det(N) / det(M)` over a field. The adjugate identity `M * adj(M) = det(M) · 1` is stated in the matrix ring `matrixRing(R, n)`, and when `det(M)` has an inverse `u`, `M * scalarMultiple(R, n, u, adj(M)) = matrixRing(R, n)[1]`. The column form and the two-sided inverse await the invariance of the determinant under transposition. Everything is in ZF.
